subject: Can you have too many surveys?

messages.author: aadb02e4fe810b70
messages.subject: Can you have too many surveys?
parts:
I have a generic (and possibly silly) question about occupancy modeling: is there ever such a thing as "too many surveys"?


I'm asking because it seems that some of the emergent "big data" survey methods (e.g. automated acoustic monitoring, camera trapping) have the opportunity to be quite survey-rich compared to traditional field studies, where folks are often hurting for surveys.


In one of these "big data" automated contexts, you could have, say, a 30 day sampling period for a single season, and be automatically collecting data every day. You could lump that data into survey periods of your choice. Maybe you define a survey as a single day (in which case, you would have an encounter history of 30 zeroes and ones). Alternatively, maybe you define a survey period as three days (in which case, you would have an encounter history of 30 days/3 = 10 zeroes and ones). Whatever you choose, you'd want to make sure your survey periods meet assumptions about closure for the target species in question.


I guess what I'm wondering is, is there ever any caution against "too many surveys"? In the example above, we're surveying for the same total time regardless -- we're just making different decisions over how to chop up that sampling period into surveys. It seems to me that the 30-survey specification would be better than the 10-survey specification, but perhaps there's a point at which too many surveys could challenge convergence or result in other unexpected behavior. 


The occupancy literature I've read is largely concerned with the problem of too few surveys, so I'm just wondering if anyone knows of any literature or practical guidelines around this!

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Can you have too many surveys?
parts:
Dear Cathleen,

I don't think this is a silly question at all.

I think that the main consideration in the context of occupancy models is closure as you say. If closure is not a problem, then possibly you get such a high, combined detection probability that you may forget about modeling the detection process and simply fit a logistic regression to the aggregated survey result instead (i.e., to the binary indicator for whether the species is ever detected or not).

On the other hand, in the possible case that you are interested in parameters of the detection model, you would of course not want to do this.

I am sure there are other considerations as well.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: aadb02e4fe810b70
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Can you have too many surveys?
parts:
Hi Marc, 

That makes a lot of sense. I hadn't considered the possibility of still having a low detection probability (and wanting to model the detection process in greater detail). We'd run into a very data-greedy modeling situation in that case, and likely wouldn't have the power to estimate all of the parameters. 

Thank you for your insightful reply!

Cathleen
